meta.name: EEG Construct–Measure Knowledge Base
meta.note: Rebuilt from papers supplied by the owner: six review and methods papers on 2026-10-08, then Torontali et al. (2019), a mouse sleep study, on 2026-10-15. The earlier spreadsheet rows and the Claude-drafted starter set were removed at the owner's request. Every entry cites a source and page; claims are paraphrased, not quoted.

sources.cite: Kappenman, E. S., & Luck, S. J. (2012). ERP components: The ups and downs of brainwave recordings. In S. J. Luck & E. S. Kappenman (Eds.), The Oxford handbook of event-related potential components (pp. 3–30). Oxford University Press.
sources.title: ERP components: The ups and downs of brainwave recordings
sources.venue: The Oxford Handbook of Event-Related Potential Components, pp. 3–30
sources.scope: Defines what an ERP component is, why peaks are not components, the superposition and latency-jitter problems, forward and reverse inference, and practical ways to isolate, measure and time components.
sources.note: Read from the uncorrected first proof (2011). Page numbers follow the chapter's pagination (3–30).

sources.cite: Woodman, G. F. (2010). A brief introduction to the use of event-related potentials in studies of perception and attention. Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics, 72(8), 2031–2046.
sources.title: A brief introduction to the use of event-related potentials in studies of perception and attention
sources.scope: Walks through the visual and auditory ERP component sequence (Table 1 maps components to processes) and gives working rules on baselines, trial counts, eye movements, measurement, referencing, refractoriness and offsets.

sources.cite: Beres, A. M. (2017). Time is of the essence: A review of electroencephalography (EEG) and event-related brain potentials (ERPs) in language research. Applied Psychophysiology and Biofeedback, 42, 247–255.
sources.title: Time is of the essence: A review of EEG and ERPs in language research
sources.scope: Reviews the ERP components most used in language research (N400, P600, LAN/ELAN, MMN) and the practical advantages and limits of ERPs for language studies.

sources.cite: Herrmann, C. S., Strüber, D., Helfrich, R. F., & Engel, A. K. (2016). EEG oscillations: From correlation to causality. International Journal of Psychophysiology, 103, 12–21.
sources.title: EEG oscillations: From correlation to causality
sources.scope: Summarizes the cognitive correlates of delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma oscillations and the methods that test causality: rhythmic sensory stimulation, neurofeedback, rTMS and tACS.

sources.cite: Gupta, D. S., & Chen, L. (2016). Brain oscillations in perception, timing and action. Current Opinion in Behavioral Sciences, 8, 161–166.
sources.title: Brain oscillations in perception, timing and action
sources.scope: Argues that coupling of gamma (local circuits) to the phase of slower oscillations creates temporal windows of integration for perception, timing and action, and reviews alpha and beta findings in that light.
sources.note: Short opinion piece; much of the cited evidence is intracranial or animal work.

sources.cite: Buzsáki, G., & Draguhn, A. (2004). Neuronal oscillations in cortical networks. Science, 304(5679), 1926–1929.
sources.title: Neuronal oscillations in cortical networks
sources.scope: Describes the system of brain oscillators from 0.05 to 500 Hz, the 1/f power spectrum, and proposed functions such as input selection, binding of cell assemblies, consolidation and phase coding.
sources.note: Evidence is mainly from rodent and intracranial recordings rather than human scalp EEG.

sources.cite: Torontali, Z. A., Fraigne, J. J., Sanghera, P., Horner, R., & Peever, J. (2019). The sublaterodorsal tegmental nucleus functions to couple brain state and motor activity during REM sleep and wakefulness. Current Biology, 29, 3803–3813.e5.
sources.title: The sublaterodorsal tegmental nucleus functions to couple brain state and motor activity during REM sleep and wakefulness
sources.scope: Chemogenetic activation and silencing of the sublaterodorsal tegmental nucleus (SLD) in narcoleptic (orexin knockout) and wild-type mice. Cortical EEG, neck and jaw EMG, and video were used to score wakefulness, NREM sleep, REM sleep, cataplexy and sleep attacks.
sources.note: Mouse study. EEG came from skull screws over frontal and parietal cortex, so the recording sites do not map onto human 10–20 electrodes.

guidance.t: Show at least 100 ms of prestimulus baseline in figures and check that baseline differences are clearly smaller than the effect of interest.
Plan trials per condition per participant by component: C1 over 1,000; P1 and N1 300–1,000; N2pc about 250; P3 about 35–60.
Sentence-processing studies with about 20 participants typically need at least 40 trials per condition.
Jitter the intertrial interval so alpha does not phase-lock to stimulation, shield the recording, and keep participants alert with short blocks and breaks (about 5–7 minute blocks).
Exclude trials with blinks and eye movements rather than relying only on correction; record EOG, and use an eye tracker when absolute fixation matters.
Keep stimulus manipulations orthogonal to attention manipulations so physically different stimuli do not masquerade as attention effects.
Measure amplitude as mean voltage (or area) in a broad window chosen in advance, and latency with fractional-area or 50%-area measures rather than peaks.
Report the reference. Avoid a Cz reference when measuring components with central maxima such as the P3 and ERN.
Space stimulus onsets about 1 s apart where possible and equate stimuli and ISIs across conditions, because early components are refractory.
Present visual stimuli briefly (about 200 ms or less) or long enough that offset responses do not overlap onset components.

Isolate components with difference waves (contralateral-minus-ipsilateral, deviant-minus-standard, rare-minus-frequent), and remember that a difference wave cannot say which original waveform changed.
Identify a component by converging evidence: polarity, latency, scalp distribution and sensitivity to manipulations together, not any one of them.
Treat reverse inference as probabilistic: the presence of a component suggests its process but does not prove it; absence can be stronger evidence if the link is well established.
Expect large individual differences in waveform shape (cortical folding, skull); grand averages from adequate samples are stable, but pilots with a few participants can mislead.
Do not assume a frequency band reflects the same process across experiments; causal claims about oscillations need modulation (rhythmic stimulation, neurofeedback, rTMS or tACS).
When two conditions' waveforms diverge, that time is an upper bound on when the brain distinguished them, not the moment processing began.
Score sleep and wake in short fixed epochs (5 s in this study), and give an epoch that spans two states the state that fills most of it.
Muscle atonia occurs in both REM sleep and cataplexy, so record video in sync with EEG and EMG and use behaviour, muscle twitches and the EEG spectrum to tell them apart.

measures.name: Contingent negative variation (CNV)
measures.spec: Slow negative shift that builds up before a stimulus the participant must respond to; includes orienting (O) and expectancy (E) waves.
measures.windowNote: Before the imperative stimulus (no window given in the sources)
measures.sitesNote: Not given in the sources

caveats.t: In studies of stimulus-evoked activity, anticipatory activity like the CNV can differ between trial types and contaminate the baseline; randomize trial types and baseline-correct.

feasibility.note: Builds up before a stimulus that requires a response.

measures.name: C1
measures.spec: First visual ERP deflection, peaking about 50–70 ms; positive or negative depending on whether the stimulus is in the upper or lower visual field.
measures.sitesNote: Occipitotemporal sites in Woodman's Fig. 1; no electrodes named

caveats.t: Reverses polarity for upper versus lower visual-field stimuli because of how primary visual cortex is folded; both polarities are the same component.
Small, overlaps the P1 and shares the frequency range of alpha noise, so a good individual measure can need over 1,000 artifact-free trials per condition.

measures.name: Visual P1 (P100)
measures.spec: Positive deflection about 90–100 ms after a visual stimulus as information moves through the visual system.
measures.sitesNote: Occipitotemporal sites in Woodman's Fig. 1; no electrodes named

caveats.t: Physically different stimuli change P1 amplitude on their own; attention effects can only be claimed when the same stimuli contribute to attended and unattended conditions.
Needs roughly 300–1,000 trials per condition to measure reliably because it overlaps alpha-band noise.
Waveform shape varies widely across healthy individuals, likely from cortical folding and skull differences rather than processing.

measures.name: Visual N1 / N170 (N100)
measures.spec: Negative deflection peaking about 170–200 ms, with posterior and anterior subtypes; the N170 is the face-sensitive variant. Beres labels the early negativity to words and pictures N100.
measures.windowNote: Peak latency N170–200 in Woodman (2010); about 100 ms in Beres (2017, Fig. 3)
measures.sitesNote: Posterior (occipitotemporal) for the posterior N1; no electrodes named

caveats.t: Same physical stimulus confound as the P1: attended and unattended conditions must use the same stimuli.
Refractory at short interstimulus intervals; Woodman's rule of thumb is to space onsets about 1 s apart.
The N170's polarity reversal across the head is easy to see, a reminder that every component is positive on one side and negative on the other.

measures.name: P2 (P200)
measures.spec: Positive deflection following the N1, about 200 ms.
measures.windowNote: About 200 ms in Beres (2017, Fig. 3); no window given in Woodman (2010)
measures.sitesNote: Not given in the sources

caveats.t: Its function is listed as not well understood.
Like the P3b, P2 amplitude depends on target probability, so a probability manipulation alone does not isolate either component.
Auditory N1 and P2 shrink when stimuli are about 1 s apart compared with longer intervals; the P3 does not.
In auditory oddball designs the P2 overlaps the MMN interval, which is why the MMN is measured from a difference wave.

measures.name: N2 (N2 family)
measures.spec: Negative deflection peaking about 225–250 ms; a family of subcomponents (N2a, N2b, N2c, N2pc) that share polarity and timing but reflect different processes.
measures.sitesNote: Not given in the sources

caveats.t: Overlaps the larger P3: an apparent N2 change can be an earlier P3 onset. Use scalp distribution to tell them apart.

measures.name: N2pc (PCN)
measures.spec: Contralateral-minus-ipsilateral negativity at occipitotemporal sites about 200 ms after a lateralized target appears among distractors.
measures.sitesNote: Occipitotemporal, contralateral minus ipsilateral to the target; electrodes not named

caveats.t: Requires distractors: it is observed for a target surrounded by distractors but not for a target shown alone.
Largely unaffected by target probability, unlike the P3b.
Eye movements toward the target shift both the corneoretinal potential and the visual input; exclude them (EOG, and an eye tracker for absolute fixation).

methods.t: About 250 trials per condition per participant.
Isolate with a contralateral-minus-ipsilateral difference wave.

measures.name: P3 / P300 (P3a, P3b)
measures.spec: Large positive wave (often over 10 µV) with a broad central-to-parietal maximum; frontally distributed P3a versus centroparietal P3b. Larger for rare targets, and its latency can vary by hundreds of milliseconds.
measures.windowNote: Named P300, but latency varies by hundreds of ms across conditions
measures.sitesNote: Broad, central to centroparietal maximum (P3b); frontal for P3a

caveats.t: Probability-sensitive, like the P2; isolate it with rare-minus-frequent difference waves.
Do not use a Cz reference for components with central maxima such as the P3.
Its timing makes peak latency a weak measure; a fractional or 50%-area latency of the difference wave is more informative.

methods.t: About 35–60 trials per condition per participant are usually enough.
Not reduced at about 1 s interstimulus intervals, unlike the auditory N1 and P2.
Composed mainly of delta and theta oscillations.

measures.name: Contralateral delay activity (CDA / SPCN)
measures.spec: Sustained posterior negativity contralateral to the remembered items during the retention interval of a lateralized visual working-memory task.
measures.sitesNote: Posterior, contralateral versus ipsilateral; electrodes not named

caveats.t: Individual differences in ERP amplitude can come from cortical folding and skull properties; the CDA is an example where they also track a cognitive ability.

measures.name: Lateralized readiness potential (LRP)
measures.spec: Difference wave: voltage at sites contralateral minus ipsilateral to the responding hand, developing before the response.
measures.sitesNote: Contralateral versus ipsilateral to the response hand; sites not named

caveats.t: A smaller LRP could mean less contralateral activity, more ipsilateral activity, or a latency difference between the two waveforms.

methods.t: Its distinctive lateralized distribution is strong (not infallible) evidence that the LRP is present.

feasibility.note: Defined relative to the responding hand, so a response is needed.

measures.name: Error-related negativity (ERN/Ne) and feedback negativity (FBN)
measures.spec: Medial frontal negativity within about 100 ms after an incorrect response, with a broad, centrally maximal distribution; the feedback negativity follows feedback.
measures.sitesNote: Medial frontal, broad with central maxima; electrodes not named

caveats.t: A Cz reference shrinks components with central maxima such as the ERN.

measures.name: Error positivity (Pe)
measures.spec: Positive deflection after errors, following the ERN.
measures.sitesNote: Not given in the sources

measures.name: Mismatch negativity (MMN)
measures.spec: Deviant-minus-standard difference wave in an auditory oddball, more negative for deviants from about 100–200 ms and peaking about 160–220 ms, fronto-central (Fz).
measures.windowNote: Difference about 100–200 ms (Kappenman & Luck, Fig. 1.6); peak 160–220 ms (Beres)
measures.sitesNote: Fz

caveats.t: Measure it from the difference wave: the P2 overlaps this interval, so the raw waveform may show no negative peak at all.

methods.t: Example design: a 1000 Hz standard on 80% of trials and deviant pitches on 20%, one tone every 1000 ms.

feasibility.note: Elicited without a task (reading, watching a film, sleeping) and used with neonates and infants.

measures.name: N400
measures.spec: Negative wave peaking about 400 ms (present 300–600 ms) for words that mismatch their semantic context; centro-parietal for written words, more fronto-central for pictures, earlier and more frontal for spoken words.
measures.windowNote: Present 300–600 ms (Kappenman & Luck); peaks about 400 ms (Beres)
measures.sitesNote: Centro-parietal for written words

caveats.t: Many components are active between 300 and 600 ms, so a deflection there is weak evidence of an N400 on its own.
An apparent increase in N400 amplitude might really be a decrease in an overlapping P3.
Topography changes with stimulus type: modality-dependent but not modality-specific.
Behavioural reaction times and N400 effects rarely pattern together.

methods.t: With about 20 participants, sentence studies need at least 40 trials per condition.
Present sentences word by word (often about 500 ms per word) to avoid eye movements and time-lock to the target word.

measures.name: P600 (syntactic positive shift)
measures.spec: Positive wave about 500–800 ms after a target word in syntactically incorrect or non-preferred sentences.
measures.sitesNote: Not given in the sources

caveats.t: It took considerable work to show that the P600 to syntactic anomalies is different from the P3.
Also elicited by violations of expected structure in music, arithmetic and sequences, so it is not specific to syntax.

measures.name: Left anterior negativity (LAN)
measures.spec: Negativity about 300–500 ms over the left frontal scalp to grammatical violations.
measures.sitesNote: Left frontal; location inconsistent across studies

caveats.t: Its scalp location has not been consistent across studies.
Debated whether it is syntax-specific or a more general index of working-memory load.

methods.t: Often followed by a P600, which is thought to reflect later integration and repair.

measures.name: Early left anterior negativity (ELAN)
measures.spec: Early negativity about 100–200 ms to phrase-structure or word-category violations, such as a participle where a noun should follow a determiner.
measures.sitesNote: Early left anterior; electrodes not named

measures.name: Late positive potential (LPP)
measures.spec: Long-lasting positivity used in emotion research, spanning hundreds of milliseconds.
measures.sitesNote: Not given in the sources

caveats.t: May be several distinct shorter components rather than one long one.
Emotional and neutral stimulus sets must be matched on physical properties for differences to reflect emotional content.

measures.name: Auditory brainstem responses (waves I–VI)
measures.spec: Very early waves within about 10 ms of a brief sound, generated in the brainstem, before the middle-latency and cortical components.
measures.windowNote: First ~10 ms on Woodman's log-time plot (Fig. 2)
measures.sitesNote: Central site (Cz) in Woodman's Fig. 2

methods.t: Elicited with a rapid sequence of clicks; amplitude and latency are compared with normal responses.

feasibility.note: Recorded in newborns without any task.

measures.name: Auditory N1
measures.spec: Negative cortical deflection after sound onset, recorded centrally; a family of subcomponents, one of which comes from tonotopically mapped auditory cortex.
measures.windowNote: No window given numerically (follows the middle-latency waves in Woodman's Fig. 2)
measures.sitesNote: Central site (Cz) in Woodman's Fig. 2

caveats.t: Refractory: N1 and P2 are reduced even about 1 s after the previous sound, and N1 refractoriness may last tens of seconds. Space onsets and equate ISIs across conditions.
Sound offsets also elicit components; brief or well-separated stimuli avoid overlap.
Scalp distribution changes with pitch because of the tonotopic subcomponent.

measures.name: Condition-difference onset latency
measures.spec: The earliest time at which ERPs from two matched conditions diverge, measured without assigning the difference to a particular component.
measures.sitesNote: Any; depends on the comparison

caveats.t: Gives an upper bound: the brain may have distinguished the conditions earlier in activity that is invisible at the scalp.
All other factors, including physical stimulus properties, must be matched between the conditions.

measures.name: Delta oscillations
measures.spec: Slow event-related oscillations below about 4 Hz; the P3 is composed mainly of delta and theta activity.
measures.bandsNote: 0–3.5 Hz as named by Walter (1936), in Herrmann et al.; 1.5–4 Hz in rat cortex (Buzsáki & Draguhn, Fig. 1)
measures.sitesNote: Sources in frontal and cingulate cortex (source level, not electrodes)

caveats.t: There is no one-to-one mapping between frequency bands and cognitive functions; the function depends on where and with what parameters the oscillation occurs.

measures.name: Theta oscillations
measures.spec: Oscillations at roughly 4–8 Hz. Frontal midline theta is used in neurofeedback and executive-control work; hippocampal theta is recorded intracranially in animals.
measures.bandsNote: 4–7.5 Hz (Walter, 1936, in Herrmann et al.); 4–8 Hz (Gupta & Chen); 4–10 Hz in rat hippocampus (Buzsáki & Draguhn)
measures.sitesNote: Frontal midline electrodes for neurofeedback (Herrmann et al., Fig. 3)

caveats.t: Theta in one experiment may reflect a very different process from theta in another; a frequency band is not a component.
There is no one-to-one mapping between frequency bands and cognitive functions.
Phase-precession and plasticity evidence comes from rodent hippocampal recordings, not human scalp EEG.

measures.name: Alpha power (8–12 Hz)
measures.spec: Power of the 8–12 Hz rhythm, the first EEG pattern described and the dominant rhythm of the raw EEG.
measures.sitesNote: Occipital origin favoured by Adrian & Matthews (1934), in Herrmann et al.

caveats.t: The largest noise source for early ERPs; it grows when participants are sleepy or bored.
There is no one-to-one mapping between frequency bands and cognitive functions.
In a sham condition, alpha first dropped with visual stimulation and then rose over the session, probably reflecting declining vigilance.

methods.t: Jitter the intertrial interval so alpha does not phase-lock to the stimulation rate.

measures.name: Prestimulus alpha power and alpha connectivity
measures.spec: Alpha power (and frontal-to-occipital alpha connectivity) in the interval before a stimulus, used to predict how the stimulus will be perceived.
measures.windowNote: Before the stimulus (about 330 ms before in the audio-tactile study)
measures.sitesNote: Superior and inferior parietal lobules; frontal and occipital regions (source level)

caveats.t: Findings come from a short opinion review summarizing single studies.

measures.name: Individual alpha frequency (alpha peak frequency)
measures.spec: Each person's peak frequency within the alpha band, measured over occipital cortex.
measures.sitesNote: Occipital alpha

caveats.t: During 10 Hz tACS the alpha peak narrowed, suggesting individual alpha frequencies shifted toward 10 Hz; stimulation can change the measure itself.

measures.name: Beta oscillations
measures.spec: Faster oscillations found predominantly over sensory-motor areas, independent of the alpha sources.
measures.bandsNote: Herrmann et al. describe Berger's beta as 20–30 Hz; rat cortex classes put beta at 10–30 Hz (Buzsáki & Draguhn). Define the band before analysis.
measures.sitesNote: Predominantly over sensory-motor areas

caveats.t: Beta was long regarded by many as muscle artifact before a cortical origin was shown.
There is no one-to-one mapping between frequency bands and cognitive functions.

measures.name: Gamma oscillations
measures.spec: Fast oscillations (about 30–80 Hz, extending to 150 Hz as high gamma) reflecting local circuit activity.
measures.bandsNote: 30–80 Hz (Buzsáki & Draguhn, Fig. 1); 30–150 Hz including high gamma (Gupta & Chen)
measures.sitesNote: Region-specific

caveats.t: Miniature saccades can produce transient induced gamma in scalp EEG.
The binding-by-gamma idea is supported by many experiments but not all.
There is no one-to-one mapping between frequency bands and cognitive functions.

measures.name: Steady-state evoked potentials (SSEP / SSVEP)
measures.spec: Response at the stimulation frequency when a stimulus is repeated rhythmically; works from about 1 to 100 Hz. First recorded over the occipital lobe with flicker by Adrian & Matthews (1934).
measures.sitesNote: Occipital for visual flicker

caveats.t: Can only drive sensory cortices.
Entrained oscillations can continue for a few cycles after stimulation ends.

feasibility.note: Elicited whenever a stimulus is presented repetitively.

measures.name: Cross-frequency phase–amplitude coupling
measures.spec: How strongly the phase of a slow rhythm (theta 4–8 Hz or alpha 8–12 Hz) modulates the amplitude of gamma (30–150 Hz).
measures.sitesNote: Region-specific

caveats.t: The direction of influence (whether gamma drives the slow rhythm or the reverse) was unresolved.
Many of the studies cited for coupling used intracranial (ECoG, LFP) or animal recordings rather than scalp EEG.

measures.name: Sleep oscillations (thalamocortical spindles)
measures.spec: Self-organized thalamocortical oscillations of the sleeping brain, including spindles.
measures.bandsNote: Band not given in the source
measures.sitesNote: Not given in the source

caveats.t: Evidence in this source is largely from animal and intracranial work.

measures.name: EEG–EMG sleep–wake scoring
measures.spec: Each 5 s epoch of cortical EEG and muscle (EMG) activity is labelled wake, NREM sleep or REM sleep. Wake shows low-amplitude, fast EEG with moderate to high EMG; NREM shows high-amplitude slow waves with little EMG; REM shows theta-rich EEG with muscle atonia broken by brief twitches.
measures.windowNote: Scored in 5 s epochs over 3 h recordings
measures.bandsNote: No band edges given for wake, NREM or REM; the EEG is described as fast, slow-wave or theta-rich
measures.sitesNote: Mouse skull screws over frontal and parietal cortex; EMG from neck and jaw (masseter) muscles

caveats.t: These criteria are for mice recorded with skull-screw EEG and neck EMG; the paper does not test them in people.
Muscle atonia alone cannot separate REM sleep from cataplexy; the paper also compared the EEG spectrum, muscle twitches, episode length and behaviour.

methods.t: EEG digitised at 1000 Hz and filtered 0.1–100 Hz; EMG filtered 30–3000 Hz and rectified; a 60 Hz notch filter applied to any noisy channel in both control and treatment recordings.
Video recorded in sync with EEG and EMG to confirm each state.
States reported as percent of time, number of episodes and mean episode length over a 3 h block starting 30 min after injection.
EMG split into 10 ms bins to separate tonic muscle tone from phasic twitches.

feasibility.note: Scored from spontaneous behaviour in a recording chamber; no task is needed.

measures.name: Sleep-attack scoring (slow-wave EEG with fading neck tone)
measures.spec: An epoch is scored as a sleep attack when neck muscle tone fades gradually, the EEG shows slow waves (0–4 Hz), and the jaw (masseter) EMG stays active, often looking like chewing.
measures.bandsNote: 0–4 Hz, as given in the scoring criteria
measures.sitesNote: Mouse skull screws over frontal and parietal cortex; EMG from neck and masseter muscles

caveats.t: The paper gives sleep-attack criteria in its methods (citing Burgess, 2010) but reports no sleep-attack results.
Not the same as cataplexy: in cataplexy, paralysis intrudes into otherwise normal wakefulness, while a sleep attack shows gradual tone loss with slow-wave EEG.
These are mouse criteria; the paper does not test them in people.

methods.t: Record jaw (masseter) EMG as well as neck EMG; masseter activity is one of the three criteria.

feasibility.note: Scored from spontaneous behaviour; no task is needed.

measures.name: EEG power spectrum of a behavioural state
measures.spec: Relative EEG power across 0–20 Hz, computed with a fast Fourier transform and compared between episodes to test whether two behavioural states are the same.
measures.bandsNote: 0–20 Hz is the range plotted in the paper (Fig. 3I)
measures.sitesNote: Mouse skull screws over frontal and parietal cortex

caveats.t: Spectral similarity was one of five lines of evidence; behaviour before and after each episode, response to touch, episode length and muscle twitches were also compared.

methods.t: Spectra compared across frequency with a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc tests.

constructs.name: Auditory brainstem transmission
constructs.definition: The earliest neural responses to sound, generated in the brainstem within about 10 ms.

constructs.name: Tonotopic encoding of sound frequency
constructs.definition: Pitch-dependent activity in tonotopically mapped auditory cortex.

constructs.name: Auditory change (deviance) detection
constructs.definition: Automatic registration that an incoming sound differs from a sensory-memory trace of the preceding sounds.

constructs.name: Covert deployment of visual attention
constructs.definition: Shifting attention to a peripheral target without moving the eyes.

constructs.name: Attention to a target among distractors
constructs.definition: Operations applied to an attended object when distractors are present.

constructs.name: Early (sensory-level) attentional selection
constructs.definition: Attention changing sensory processing within the first ~100 ms, as early-selection models propose.

constructs.name: Anticipation and preparation
constructs.definition: Cognitive and motor preparation for an expected stimulus that requires a response.

constructs.name: Target detection among distractors
constructs.definition: Detecting a target or go-stimulus in a series of distractors or no-go stimuli.

constructs.name: Inhibition of task-irrelevant input
constructs.definition: Suppressing stimuli, locations or cortical regions that the task does not need.

constructs.name: Attentional processes (general)
constructs.definition: Attention as a broad function, without a more specific mechanism named in the source.

constructs.name: Attentive processing of information
constructs.definition: Enhanced processing of attended information.

constructs.name: Pre-attentive processing
constructs.definition: Processing that runs without directed attention or a task, for example during sleep, while reading, or in coma.

constructs.name: Visual working memory maintenance
constructs.definition: Holding visual information in working memory over a short delay.

constructs.name: Visual working memory capacity
constructs.definition: How much visual information an individual can store at once.

constructs.name: Controlling access to working memory
constructs.definition: Keeping irrelevant stimuli from being stored.

constructs.name: Context (working memory) updating
constructs.definition: Revising the current representation of the task context when a relevant event occurs.

constructs.name: Working memory encoding
constructs.definition: Entering a stimulus into working memory.

constructs.name: Memory processes (general)
constructs.definition: Memory as a broad function, without a more specific stage named in the source.

constructs.name: Working memory retention and mental imagery
constructs.definition: Keeping information active, or generating images, using distributed cortical areas.

constructs.name: Working memory performance
constructs.definition: Speed and capacity on working-memory tasks.

constructs.name: Working memory capacity limit (theta–gamma code)
constructs.definition: The idea that the number of items held is set by how many gamma cycles fit in one theta cycle.

constructs.name: Active maintenance of memory contents
constructs.definition: Keeping specific memory contents active.

constructs.name: Recognition memory
constructs.definition: Recognizing previously studied material.

constructs.name: Sleep-dependent memory consolidation
constructs.definition: Turning recently learned information into long-term memory during sleep.

constructs.name: Spatial representation by spike phase
constructs.definition: Encoding an animal's position in the theta phase at which hippocampal place cells fire.

constructs.name: Phase-dependent synaptic plasticity
constructs.definition: Whether synapses strengthen or weaken depending on the oscillation phase at which input arrives.

constructs.name: Working memory load
constructs.definition: The amount of information working memory must hold during processing.

constructs.name: Semantic processing (integration of meaning)
constructs.definition: Processing a word's meaning and integrating it with its context.

constructs.name: Semantic memory
constructs.definition: How knowledge of meaning is stored and retrieved.

constructs.name: Word perception
constructs.definition: Perceiving a word well enough for its meaning to interact with context.

constructs.name: Syntactic processing (violation, reanalysis, integration)
constructs.definition: Processing sentence structure, including detecting violations and reanalyzing or integrating difficult structures.

constructs.name: Monitoring of expected structure
constructs.definition: Detecting and re-evaluating violations of an expected structure, linguistic or not (music, arithmetic, sequences).

constructs.name: Morpho-syntactic agreement processing
constructs.definition: Checking grammatical agreement, for example between subject and verb.

constructs.name: Phrase-structure building
constructs.definition: Fast, automatic use of word-category information to build phrase structure.

constructs.name: Native-language phoneme discrimination (development)
constructs.definition: Infants' ability to distinguish speech sounds, which narrows toward native-language contrasts in the first year.

constructs.name: Emotional content processing
constructs.definition: Processing that distinguishes emotion-evoking from neutral stimuli.

constructs.name: Error processing and detection
constructs.definition: Registering that a response was wrong.

constructs.name: Response-conflict monitoring
constructs.definition: Detecting conflict between competing responses.

constructs.name: Reinforcement learning (feedback)
constructs.definition: Learning from outcomes and feedback.

constructs.name: Conscious or affective evaluation of performance
constructs.definition: Awareness of, or an affective reaction to, one's own performance.

constructs.name: Functional inhibition in executive control
constructs.definition: Frontal regulation of other brain structures through inhibition.

constructs.name: Cognitive load
constructs.definition: Demand placed on limited processing resources.

constructs.name: Response selection and preparation
constructs.definition: Choosing which response to make and preparing it.

constructs.name: Response activation by unseen stimuli
constructs.definition: Preparation of a response triggered by a stimulus the person is not aware of.

constructs.name: Motor execution (movement)
constructs.definition: Carrying out movements.

constructs.name: Maintaining the current sensorimotor state
constructs.definition: Signalling whether the current sensorimotor state is expected to stay stable or change.

constructs.name: Sensorimotor integration
constructs.definition: Tight temporal coordination of perception and action across distributed circuits.

constructs.name: Interval timing and time estimation
constructs.definition: Representing the duration of time intervals.

constructs.name: Early visual sensory processing
constructs.definition: The first feedforward sweep of visual information through visual cortex.

constructs.name: Low-level, automatic perception
constructs.definition: Basic perceptual processing that occurs whenever a stimulus is shown.

constructs.name: Visual discrimination
constructs.definition: Discriminating between visual stimuli.

constructs.name: Face and expert object recognition
constructs.definition: Recognizing faces and objects of expertise.

constructs.name: Object recognition and categorization
constructs.definition: Recognizing what an object is and assigning it to a category.

constructs.name: Stimulus evaluation and categorization
constructs.definition: Evaluating a stimulus and deciding which category it belongs to.

constructs.name: Conscious perception
constructs.definition: Perceiving a stimulus consciously.

constructs.name: Feature binding
constructs.definition: Combining separately processed features into one coherent percept.

constructs.name: Visual perception (input regulation)
constructs.definition: How well visual input is perceived, regulated by ongoing rhythms.

constructs.name: Near-threshold perception
constructs.definition: Detecting stimuli close to the perceptual threshold.

constructs.name: Multisensory temporal integration
constructs.definition: Combining inputs from different senses that arrive within a temporal window.

constructs.name: Temporal resolution of visual perception
constructs.definition: How finely the visual system separates events in time.

constructs.name: Apparent motion perception
constructs.definition: Perceiving motion when two static objects alternate in sequence.

constructs.name: Bistable motion perception
constructs.definition: Which of two interpretations of an ambiguous motion display is perceived.

constructs.name: Sensory processing (general)
constructs.definition: Processing of sensory stimulation, without a more specific stage named in the source.

constructs.name: Processing without awareness (masking)
constructs.definition: How far a stimulus is processed when masking keeps it out of awareness.

constructs.name: Vigilance and alertness
constructs.definition: How alert or drowsy a participant is.

constructs.name: Local cortical activation
constructs.definition: Activity within local cortical circuits, related to neuronal spiking.

constructs.name: Long-range coordination between regions
constructs.definition: Synchronizing activity across large or distant cortical areas.

constructs.name: Entrainment of brain rhythms
constructs.definition: Driving brain oscillations to follow an external rhythm.

constructs.name: Sleep deepening (sensory disconnection)
constructs.definition: Reducing the influence of the environment on the cortex as sleep deepens.

constructs.name: Hearing-loss screening in newborns
constructs.definition: Checking whether early sensory responses to sound are abnormal in infants who cannot respond behaviourally.

constructs.name: Brain–computer interface communication
constructs.definition: Using brain responses to let people who cannot move communicate.

constructs.name: When the brain distinguishes two conditions
constructs.definition: The time by which neural processing differs between two conditions.

constructs.name: Sleep–wake state (wake, NREM, REM)
constructs.definition: Which behavioural state an animal is in, identified from brain and muscle activity together: wakefulness, non-REM sleep or REM sleep.

constructs.name: Sleep attacks
constructs.definition: Episodes scored when neck muscle tone fades gradually while the EEG shows slow waves and jaw-muscle activity continues.

constructs.name: Cataplexy (paralysis during wakefulness)
constructs.definition: Sudden, involuntary muscle paralysis or weakness that intrudes into otherwise normal wakefulness; a symptom of narcolepsy.

entries.claim: Listed as the component that precedes a stimulus, indexing anticipation and cognitive and motor preparation; described as the first cognitive ERP component found once averaging became available.
entries.paradigm: A stimulus that requires a response, after a preparation period
entries.cites: Walter et al. (1964); Brunia, van Boxtel & Böcker (in press)

entries.claim: Reflects sensory processing at about 50–70 ms; thought to arise in primary visual cortex and assumed to be wholly or mainly feedforward.
entries.cites: Clark, Fan & Hillyard (1995); Jeffreys & Axford (1972); Zhang & Luck (2008)

entries.claim: Reflects sensory and perceptual processing at about 90–100 ms as information moves through the visual system; assumed to be largely feedforward.
entries.cites: Heinze et al. (1994); Luck (1995); Vogel & Luck (2000)

entries.claim: Many studies report P1 and N1 modulations when attention is allocated to locations and stimuli, provided the same stimuli contribute to attended and unattended conditions.
entries.paradigm: Spatial or feature-based attention with stimuli counterbalanced across conditions

entries.claim: N1 is modulated, like the P1, when attention is allocated to locations and stimuli, provided the stimuli are identical across attention conditions.
entries.paradigm: Spatial or feature-based attention with stimuli counterbalanced across conditions

entries.claim: N1 (about 170–200 ms) is linked to perceptual processing and visual discrimination.
The N170 variant is face-sensitive and is linked to expert recognition.
Early components (P100, N100, P200) reflect basic, low-level perception and are thought to be automatic, appearing whenever a perceptual stimulus is presented.
Early components (P100, N100, P200) reflect basic, low-level perception and are thought to be automatic, appearing whenever a perceptual stimulus is presented.
Early components (P100, N100, P200) reflect basic, low-level perception and are thought to be automatic, appearing whenever a perceptual stimulus is presented.
N2 (about 225–250 ms) is associated with object recognition and categorization; best treated as one of a family of N2 components.
entries.cites: Folstein & Van Petten (2008); Pritchard, Shappell & Brandt (1991)

entries.claim: Indexes the deployment of covert attention to peripheral targets. Its timing (about 200 ms) and distribution suggest feedback from an attentional control structure.
entries.cites: Eimer (1996); Luck & Hillyard (1994a, 1994b); Cohen et al. (2009)

entries.claim: First proposed to reflect filtering of distractors; later evidence indicates it reflects operations applied to the attended object when distractors are present. The evidence so far suggests it appears if and only if attention is allocated to an object among distractors.
entries.paradigm: Visual search; target alone versus among distractors
entries.cites: Luck & Hillyard (1994); Luck et al. (1997); Hickey, Di Lollo & McDonald (2009)

entries.claim: Used to test whether covert shifts of visual attention are delayed in schizophrenia, isolated with contralateral-minus-ipsilateral difference waves.
Object-substitution masking did not eliminate the N2pc, showing that attention still oriented to a target the participant failed to report.
P3 is linked to stimulus evaluation time and categorization.
P3 is linked to context (working memory) updating; with the CDA it indexes working-memory encoding and maintenance.
Listed among the processes the P3 indexes: cognitive load.

The onset of the rare-minus-frequent P3b difference marks when the brain has begun to categorize the stimulus. In schizophrenia this difference was not delayed despite about 60 ms slower responses, pointing to slowing after categorization.
entries.paradigm: Oddball with letters and digits (one category rare, p = .2)
entries.cites: Kutas, McCarthy & Donchin (1977); Luck et al. (2009)

entries.claim: Assuming working-memory encoding produces a P3, its absence during the attentional blink was taken to show no encoding occurred; the conclusion is only as sound as that assumption.
ERPs have been used to build brain–computer interfaces that let patients with ALS communicate with family and caregivers; the cited study used a P300-based interface.
The CDA (also called SPCN) indexes maintenance of information in visual working memory.
CDA amplitude predicts an individual's ability to store information in visual working memory.
CDA amplitude also predicts how well an individual avoids storing irrelevant stimuli.
Indexes selection and preparation of the motor response.
entries.paradigm: Choice task with left- and right-hand responses

entries.claim: The contralateral-minus-ipsilateral difference isolates response-selection activity. In schizophrenia the LRP was smaller and later, supporting slowed processing after stimulus categorization.
entries.paradigm: Oddball with letters and digits, two-hand responses

entries.claim: Stimuli associated with a response activate preparation of that response, as indexed by the LRP, even when the participant is unaware of the stimulus and does not respond.
A medial frontal negativity after the response, linked to error processing.
entries.cites: Falkenstein et al. (2000); Gehring et al. (in press)

entries.claim: Listed (with the feedback negativity) as a possible reinforcement-learning signal.
Listed as a possible response-conflict signal.
Occurs within about 100 ms of an error response and revealed a process that behavioural measures could not capture, which focused research on error detection.
The ERN also led to a large literature on response-conflict monitoring.
Listed as reflecting affective or conscious assessment of task performance.
When a deviant pitch differs enough from the standard, the ERP is more negative for the deviant from about 100 to 200 ms; this is quantified from the deviant-minus-standard difference wave.
entries.paradigm: 1000 Hz standard on 80% of trials, deviant pitches on 20%, one tone every 1000 ms

entries.claim: Reflects auditory deviance in an oddball sequence, peaking about 160–220 ms, and is thought to come from an automatic comparison of incoming sounds with a sensory-memory trace of previous sounds.
Suggested to act pre-attentively, because it can be elicited in coma and while listening to music, watching a film, reading or sleeping, without any specific task.

Finnish infants showed a larger MMN to a non-native Estonian vowel at 7 months than at 11 months, so sensitivity to non-native contrasts declines; adults show smaller MMNs to non-native vowel categories.
entries.cites: Cheour et al. (1998); Näätänen et al. (1997)

entries.claim: Widely used to assess infants' ability to make complex perceptual discriminations, such as distinctions between phonemes.

First reported by Kutas and Hillyard (1980) to anomalous sentence endings and peaking about 400 ms; tied to processing meaning, since capitalized target words and simple grammatical errors do not elicit it.
entries.paradigm: Word-by-word sentences: 75% congruent endings versus strange or anomalous endings

entries.claim: Its sensitivity to meaning has supported studies of how semantic memory is stored and retrieved.
Larger for words that mismatch their semantic context (for example, nurse after cup rather than after doctor), but which process it represents is controversial.
An N400 context effect cannot occur unless the words were perceived, so its presence shows perception. This logic showed that words can be fully perceived even when unattended.
entries.cites: Luck, Vogel & Shapiro (1996); Vogel et al. (1998, 2005)

entries.claim: Object-substitution masking impaired the N400 difference between matching and mismatching words, so this masking acts after early perception but before semantic analysis.

A positive wave about 500–800 ms after a target word that indexes processing of syntactically incorrect or non-preferred sentences; larger for ungrammatical continuations than for grammatical but non-preferred ones.
entries.paradigm: Sentences with syntactic violations or garden paths
entries.cites: Osterhout & Holcomb (1992); Hagoort et al. (1993); Osterhout, Holcomb & Swinney (1994); Kaan et al. (2000)

entries.claim: Also linked to monitoring and re-evaluation, and elicited by violations in music, arithmetic and sequencing, which suggests sensitivity to any violated expected structure.
entries.paradigm: Violations in language, music, arithmetic, sequences
entries.cites: Kolk et al. (2003); Besson & Macar (1987); Patel et al. (1998); Núñez-Peña & Honrubia-Serrano (2004)

entries.claim: A great deal of work was needed to establish that the P600 elicited by syntactic anomalies is distinct from the P3.
A left frontal negativity about 300–500 ms elicited by grammatical violations; first tied to morpho-syntactic agreement, an interpretation later questioned.
entries.paradigm: Sentences with agreement or phrase-structure violations
entries.cites: Kutas & Hillyard (1983); Friederici et al. (1993, 2002); Hagoort et al. (2003); Deutsch & Bentin (2001)

entries.claim: Debated: some researchers argue the LAN is a general index of working-memory load rather than syntax-specific.
An early negativity (about 100–200 ms) implicated in automatic processing of phrase structure, elicited when phrase structure or word category is violated.
entries.paradigm: Word-category violations (e.g., a participle after a determiner)
entries.cites: Neville et al. (1991); Friederici et al. (1993)

entries.claim: Used in the emotion literature; it looks like one component lasting hundreds of milliseconds but may be made of several shorter components.
The time at which ERPs to emotional and neutral pictures diverge shows by when the brain has distinguished emotional content (an upper bound).
entries.paradigm: Emotional versus neutral pictures matched on physical properties

entries.claim: Under some conditions attended and ignored stimuli diverge within about 50 ms (auditory) and 100 ms (visual), key evidence for early-selection models of attention.
entries.cites: Hillyard, Vogel & Luck (1998); Luck, Woodman & Vogel (2000); Woldorff et al. (1993)

entries.claim: Comparing two conditions to find when their waveforms begin to diverge is a component-independent way to time processing, and requires fewer assumptions than component-based measures.
Auditory stimuli elicit very early waves, generated in the brainstem, before the middle-latency and cortical components.
entries.paradigm: Brief auditory stimulus; Cz; log-time plot

entries.claim: For many years the amplitude and latency of early brainstem responses to rapid clicks have been used to check whether newborns have hearing loss.
One subcomponent of the auditory N1 arises from tonotopically mapped auditory cortex, so its scalp distribution changes with the pitch of the stimulus.
The most prominent cognitive correlate of event-related delta is detecting a target or go-stimulus among distractors; the P3 to such stimuli is composed mainly of delta and theta.
Delta sources in frontal and cingulate cortex span wide networks, possibly acting through inhibition, which fits a role in attention achieved by inhibiting other stimuli or locations.
Oscillatory stimulation at a delta frequency during sleep enhanced EEG delta activity and improved recall of memory items the next morning.
Human EEG theta is most commonly associated with memory processes and may reflect communication with the hippocampus.
Theta is also seen, mainly over frontal cortex, during functional inhibition that supports executive functions.
6 Hz tACS in phase over left frontal and parietal regions shortened working-memory reaction times, and theta tACS over parietal sites increased storage capacity.
entries.cites: Polanía et al. (2012); Jaušovec, Jaušovec & Pahor (2014); Jaušovec & Jaušovec (2014)

entries.claim: Working-memory retention and mental imagery, which likely involve distributed cortical areas, are related to theta and alpha oscillations, whereas visual processing reflects local activity.
Low-frequency oscillations synchronize larger areas of cortex and support long-range interactions.

As a rat moves through a place field, hippocampal place-cell spikes shift to progressively earlier theta phases (phase precession), so position is represented by phase; interfering with theta impairs spatial learning.
entries.cites: O'Keefe & Recce (1993); Huxter, Burgess & O'Keefe (2003); Dragoi, Harris & Buzsáki (2003)

entries.claim: In the hippocampus, brief pulse trains at the peak of theta induce long-term potentiation, while the same trains out of phase weaken previously strengthened inputs.
entries.paradigm: Pulse-train stimulation timed to theta phase

entries.claim: Alpha dominates the EEG, is particularly large when observers are sleepy or bored, and decreases when a stimulus appears; it is the largest noise source for early visual ERPs.
Alpha oscillations are modulated during sensory stimulation.
Alpha oscillations reflect memory processes.
Alpha oscillations reflect attentional processes.
Alpha correlates inversely with cognitive performance, suggesting it inhibits task-irrelevant cortical structures; it may also serve as a pacemaker for timing.
Alpha-frequency rTMS has been used to demonstrate a causal role of alpha oscillations in visual perception.
Alpha-frequency rTMS likewise confirmed a role of alpha in memory processes.
A 10 Hz current over auditory cortex modulated near-threshold auditory perception in a sinusoidal manner, so the phase of stimulation matters as well as its frequency.
Working-memory retention and mental imagery are related to theta and alpha oscillations.
Low-frequency oscillations, alpha included, synchronize larger areas of cortex and support long-range interactions.

Alpha power over the superior and inferior parietal lobules was relatively higher about 330 ms before a tactile stimulus when an audio-tactile pair was later perceived as integrated rather than segregated.
Higher prestimulus alpha power predicted apparent-motion percepts at low presentation frequencies; the percept depended on local alpha power and frontal-occipital alpha connectivity.
Individual alpha peak frequency correlated with the size of the temporal window of the sound-induced double-flash illusion, and that window is constrained causally by occipital alpha frequency.
entries.cites: Cecere, Rees & Romei (2015); Shams, Kamitani & Shimojo (2000)

entries.claim: Faster alpha frequencies predict finer temporal resolution of vision.
Beta is mainly modulated when participants perform motor tasks, and also during cognitive tasks that require sensorimotor interaction.
Proposed to signal whether the current sensorimotor state is expected to remain stable or to change.
20 Hz tACS slowed voluntary movements and finger tapping, and EEG–EMG coherence at 20 Hz before movement indicated that beta is causally relevant to executing movements.
entries.paradigm: 20 Hz tACS during go/no-go and tapping tasks
entries.cites: Pogosyan et al. (2009); Joundi et al. (2012); Wach et al. (2013a)

entries.claim: Beta oscillations are implicated in representing time durations; in monkeys, putamen beta rose during the internally guided phase of a synchronization-continuation task.
entries.cites: Kononowicz & van Rijn (2015); Cirelli et al. (2014); Bartolo & Merchant (2015)

entries.claim: Unlike slower rhythms linked to inhibition, gamma oscillations are believed to reflect cortical activation.
Depending on the cortical region, gamma is closely related to attentive processing of information.
Gamma is related to active maintenance of memory contents.
Gamma is related to conscious perception.
40 Hz tACS increased interhemispheric gamma coherence and biased perception of a bistable motion display.
entries.paradigm: Antiphasic 40 Hz tACS with a bistable motion display

entries.claim: Gamma oscillations represent local activity of brain circuits and relate to neuronal spiking.
entries.cites: Burns, Xing & Shapley (2010); Schanze & Eckhorn (1997); Belitski et al. (2008)

entries.claim: Distributed assemblies linked by a common gamma rhythm could bind the attributes of an image into one percept ('binding by gamma'); numerous experiments support this, though some do not.
entries.cites: Gray et al. (1989); Engel, Fries & Singer (2001); Steriade, Amzica & Contreras (1996); Shadlen & Movshon (1999)

entries.claim: Repetitive stimulation from about 1 to 100 Hz elicits steady-state responses whose resonance frequencies resemble those of ERPs; the entrained oscillation can continue for a few cycles after stimulation.
entries.cites: Regan (1982); Herrmann (2001); Halbleib et al. (2012); Spaak, de Lange & Jensen (2014)

entries.claim: Flickering study material at 10 Hz improved recognition memory compared with 8.7 and 11.7 Hz, and brought older adults' performance close to that of younger adults.
entries.paradigm: Visual flicker during a recognition-memory task

entries.claim: When Kanizsa-figure inducers were flickered at 40 Hz, the evoked 40 Hz oscillations correlated with faster responses on trials whose flicker contained an illusory square.
entries.paradigm: 40 Hz flicker of Kanizsa inducers, then a target figure

entries.claim: Coupling of gamma amplitude (local circuits) to a specific phase of long-range theta or alpha oscillations is proposed to create temporal windows of integration that coordinate perception, timing and action.
entries.cites: Canolty et al. (2006); Lakatos et al. (2005); Voytek et al. (2010)

entries.claim: Hypothesis: the roughly seven-item working-memory limit follows from the roughly 1:7 ratio of theta to gamma cycles; theta–gamma coupling has been shown in humans.
entries.cites: Lisman & Idiart (1995); Mormann et al. (2005); Canolty et al. (2006); Demiralp et al. (2007)

entries.claim: Slow rhythms synchronize large spatial domains and can bind specific assemblies by timing faster, localized oscillations; the 1/f spectrum implies slow oscillations modulate faster local events.
Thalamocortical spindle oscillations reduce environmental influences on neocortical activity, actively shifting sleep into deeper stages.
Self-organized sleep oscillations carry spike sequences created during the previous waking period, which may be turned into long-term memory through synaptic modification.

Wake, NREM and REM sleep were scored in 5 s epochs from cortical EEG together with neck EMG: fast, low-amplitude EEG with muscle activity for wake; high-amplitude slow waves with little muscle activity for NREM; theta-rich EEG with atonia and twitches for REM.
entries.paradigm: 3 h dark-phase recordings after saline or CNO injection
entries.cites: Burgess & Peever (2013); Snow et al. (2017); Burgess (2010); Brooks & Peever (2012)

entries.claim: Theta-rich EEG, together with muscle atonia punctuated by twitches, was the criterion for scoring REM sleep.
entries.cites: Burgess & Peever (2013); Snow et al. (2017); Burgess (2010); Brooks & Peever (2012)

entries.claim: Cataplexy was scored with the consensus definition for mouse models of narcolepsy, using EEG, EMG and synchronized video together.
entries.paradigm: 3 h dark-phase recordings; running wheels and chocolate in the cage to increase cataplexy
entries.behaviour: Collapse with loss of postural muscle tone

entries.claim: Sleep attacks were scored from a gradual loss of neck muscle tone, slow waves at 0–4 Hz in the EEG, and masseter EMG activity that often resembled chewing.
entries.paradigm: Spontaneous behaviour during 3 h dark-phase recordings

entries.claim: EEG slow waves at 0–4 Hz were one of the three criteria for scoring a sleep attack.
entries.paradigm: Spontaneous behaviour during 3 h dark-phase recordings

entries.claim: EEG power during behavioural arrests triggered by activating the SLD in wild-type mice matched natural cataplexy in narcoleptic mice and differed from REM sleep; the authors used this as evidence that the arrests were cataplexy, not REM sleep.
entries.paradigm: Chemogenetic SLD activation (CNO) compared with natural cataplexy and REM sleep
entries.behaviour: Loss of postural tone; no response to touch
